nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae that base the open-water food chain around the islands. Sponges and zooplankton feed on them.

nodes.name: Reef algae
nodes.desc: Seaweeds and turf algae growing on the rocky reefs. Green turtles are herbivores that graze plant growth like this.

nodes.name: Noronha cactus
nodes.desc: A tall columnar cactus recorded very often on the island. It copes with the dry season and provides cover and fruit.

nodes.name: Crab's eye vine
nodes.desc: A climbing legume recorded on the island. GloBI lists it as food for the Common Blue butterfly.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting grazers that eat phytoplankton and are eaten by small fish.

nodes.name: Marine sponges
nodes.desc: Filter feeders on the reef that strain tiny particles from the water. They are the main food of hawksbill turtles.

nodes.name: Lanternfish
nodes.desc: Small deep-water fish that rise toward the surface at night to feed on plankton. Spinner dolphins hunt small fish of this kind.

nodes.name: Flying fish
nodes.desc: Plankton-feeding fish that glide above the waves. They make up most of the masked booby diet.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: A herbivorous turtle that feeds in shallow waters. Tiger sharks are among its recorded predators.

nodes.name: Hawksbill sea turtle
nodes.desc: Critically endangered and tied to reefs by its diet of sponges (70 to 95 percent) plus algae and invertebrates.

nodes.name: Rock cavy
nodes.desc: A rodent introduced by the military in the 1960s as game. Feral cats prey on it.

nodes.name: Common Blue butterfly
nodes.desc: A small butterfly whose caterpillars feed on legumes such as crab's eye. A source of insect food for lizards.

nodes.name: Noronha skink
nodes.desc: An endemic island lizard, the most recorded reptile near the site. Small insects are its likely food.

nodes.name: Argentine tegu
nodes.desc: Brought in the 1950s to control rats; now an invasive pest that feeds largely on bird eggs.

nodes.name: Masked booby
nodes.desc: A seabird that plunge-dives for flying fish and squid. Its eggs are open to rats and other egg predators.

nodes.name: Spinner dolphin
nodes.desc: Resident in large numbers. It eats small mesopelagic fish, squid and shrimp, and is preyed on by sharks.

nodes.name: Feral cat
nodes.desc: Domestic cats gone wild; they prey on native birds, rock cavies and rodents.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: An apex predator with a very broad diet that includes sea turtles, dolphins, seabirds and carrion.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong equatorial sun powers algae in clear shallow water and the island plants.

nodes.name: Ocean currents & nutrients
nodes.desc: Open-ocean water around the islands carries nutrients and plankton that the reefs and fish depend on.

nodes.name: Seasonal rain
nodes.desc: Island plants depend on a wet and a dry season; rain feeds the cactus and vines.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead algae, plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil and water.
